explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. "In vain" means the plotting goes nowhere. You can see it in what comes next: God laughs, and then He announces He has already installed His King on Zion (Psalm 2:4, 6). Plan after plan, and not one of them gets off the counter.

Not quite, friend. "In vain" means the plotting is empty and gets them nowhere. The psalm backs it up fast: the One in heaven laughs, and then He says, "I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain." Nobody's plan is moving that.

explanations.answer: The LORD and His Anointed One
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The psalm says the kings take their stand "against the LORD and against His Anointed One." That's the whole target of the meeting. It's a big crowd of rulers all aimed in one direction, and it's the wrong direction.

explanations.answer: Moses and the elders of Israel
explanations.explanation: That one belongs to another Bible story, friend. This psalm names the target right in verse 2: the kings gather "against the LORD and against His Anointed One." So the opponent here is much higher up than any group of elders.

explanations.answer: Elijah and the prophets of God
explanations.explanation: Good name to know, but it isn't the one in this psalm. Verse 2 says the rulers stand "against the LORD and against His Anointed One." No prophets in sight. The kings are going straight to the top.

explanations.answer: Break them and cast them away
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Their words are, "Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords." They want out, and they want it done loud. Throwing the cords away means they don't plan on picking them back up.

explanations.answer: Gather them and hold them tight
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what they say, friend. The kings want to "break Their chains and cast away Their cords." Nobody in that meeting is holding anything tight. They want to throw it all off.

explanations.answer: Bury them and leave them hidden
explanations.explanation: Close on the mood, but not the words. The kings say, "Let us break Their chains and cast away Their cords." They talk about breaking and casting away, and burying never comes up. It's more like a big throw than a quiet dig.

That's the one, baker. "The One enthroned in heaven laughs; the Lord taunts them." All that plotting down on earth, and up in heaven He laughs. I still think about that every time I plan something big.
Hold on, friend, this one's turned around. The trembling shows up later, when the kings are told to "rejoice with trembling" (Psalm 2:11). The One enthroned in heaven is the one who laughs.
Nope, nobody's hiding up there. The psalm says the One enthroned in heaven laughs and taunts the kings. He stays on His throne, and He's the calmest One in the whole psalm.
Careful, friend, the laughing isn't the end of it. The psalm says, "Then He rebukes them in His anger, and terrifies them in His fury." He doesn't let anything slide. After the laugh, He speaks.

Right, baker. After the laugh comes a rebuke: "Then He rebukes them in His anger, and terrifies them in His fury." Then He says, "I have installed My King on Zion." The kings thought they were running a meeting, and God had already answered.
That's it, baker. He says, "I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain." Notice the word "have." It's already done before the kings finish their meeting.

explanations.answer: Sent a flood over the earth
explanations.explanation: A flood is a real thing in the Bible, but it's in another story. In this psalm, God announces, "I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain." No water here, just a King already in place.
That's a different scene from a different book, friend. Here the announcement is, "I have installed My King on Zion, upon My holy mountain." He talks about a King who is already in place.

explanations.answer: He is close to the LORD like a son
explanations.explanation: Nicely done, baker. The LORD says, "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father." That's a father-and-son kind of closeness. And it's the same King He installed on Zion.

explanations.answer: He won his crown in a great battle
explanations.explanation: The psalm doesn't tell it that way, friend. The decree is a father speaking to a son: "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father." The King was installed by the LORD, and there's no battle mentioned in this psalm.

explanations.answer: He will rule for only a short time
explanations.explanation: The psalm says nothing about a short time. If anything, the next verse talks about the nations as His inheritance and "the ends of the earth Your possession." That sounds like a King with a lot of ground to cover.

That's right, friend. The LORD says, "Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance, the ends of the earth Your possession." It's a big gift, and it starts with a simple request. I can't think of a better deal on any counter.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says, "Ask Me, and I will make the nations Your inheritance, the ends of the earth Your possession." The nations and the ends of the earth are both in the offer. The Son only has to ask.
You got it, baker. "You will break them with an iron scepter; You will shatter them like pottery." A scepter is a king's rod, and iron is a strong metal. Pottery doesn't stand a chance against that.
That's a good tool, but not the one in this verse. The LORD says, "You will break them with an iron scepter." It's a king's rod, and it's made of iron.

A shield is for blocking, friend, and the verse isn't about blocking. It says, "You will break them with an iron scepter; You will shatter them like pottery." Iron, not bronze, and a scepter, not a shield.

That's the one, baker. The psalm says, "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling." After telling the kings to be wise, it tells them whom to serve. Kings who showed up to break chains are now told to serve.
No chariots in this psalm, friend. After telling the kings to be wise, it says, "Serve the LORD with fear." The advice points them to the LORD, not to their own gear.
Egypt never comes up in this psalm. The kings are told, "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling." The help they're pointed toward is the LORD Himself.

That's right, baker. The warning says the kings could "perish in your rebellion." Rebellion is exactly what they came to do back in verse 3. The psalm calls it what it is, and then it offers them a way out.
Money never comes up in this psalm, friend. The kings are warned they could "perish in your rebellion." It's about the rebelling they started when they planned to break the chains.
Exile is a real Bible word, but it isn't in this verse. The warning says the kings could "perish in your rebellion." It ties right back to their plan to break the chains.
Careful, friend, the psalm says the opposite. It says "when His wrath ignites in an instant." Nothing slow about that. It's more like a oven mitt left on a burner, but even faster.
Right, baker. The psalm says "when His wrath ignites in an instant." That's the opposite of slow. It's the reason the kings are told to act wisely now.

explanations.answer: All who take refuge in Him
explanations.explanation: That's the ending, baker. "Blessed are all who take refuge in Him." After all that warning, the last line is good news, and it's for all who take refuge. I love a psalm that finishes warm.

explanations.answer: All who rule over the earth
explanations.explanation: Nice try, friend, but ruling isn't what the psalm blesses. It says, "Blessed are all who take refuge in Him." Even kings are invited to do that, but the blessing is for taking refuge.
Crowns don't make the list, friend. The last line says, "Blessed are all who take refuge in Him." The blessing goes to those who take refuge, whoever they are.
